<reason>Both sides argued tightly and narrowed the clash to "legibility versus veto," which made the debate easy to adjudicate. CON's reframe (dubbing as licensed translation, fidelity not forgery, coercion is not cured by moving the signature, individual veto empowers stars and estates while stranding day players) was genuinely strong and consistently maintained. But PRO won the decisive exchanges. First, PRO turned CON's own bargaining-power admission [B1.6] against it: if the market is take-it-or-leave-it, that indicts buried authority even more than an itemized grant, since the performer surrenders without knowing. CON never squarely answered that symmetry beyond asserting collective power is the only remedy — while PRO had already conceded union scale and consent are complements. Second, PRO exploited CON's "itemization without veto is fine" concession with the cleanest weighing line of the debate: protections like reuse fees, deletion duties, and no-training rules must be priced, and prices require the possibility of refusal, so stripping the "no" leaves the studio negotiating with itself. Third, PRO defused the hostage/holdout scenario with timing — consent at hiring, before localization spend — which CON only restated rather than rebutted. CON's best unanswered residue is estates/deceased performers and legacy catalogs, plus the sharp "a veto doesn't delete a file," but these were asserted more than developed, and PRO's durable-asset framing ("Klaus goes home; the model doesn't") kept the distinctiveness of synthetic reuse alive. Pressure questions were handled honestly on both sides with proper A1/A2 labels; CON's candid "there isn't a buried use inside faithful dubbing" was admirable but conceded ground on scope, which PRO converted.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's conversion of CON's "itemization without veto is fine" concession into "a right you cannot refuse is not a right — it is a tariff; prices come from the possibility of refusal," combined with the earlier turn that take-it-or-leave-it bargaining indicts page-34 boilerplate more than an itemized clause.</best_rebuttal>
